items.actClause:
AN ACT to amend the public service law and the public authorities law, in
relation to providing rate payers with reimbursement following prolonged power
outages
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S4824

SPONSOR: COMRIE
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the public service law and the public authorities law,
in relation to providing rate payers with reimbursement following
prolonged power outages

 
PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL:

The purpose of this bill is to provide compensation to residential
customers of gas and electric corporations and authorities experiencing
prolonged service outages lasting longer than 48 hours.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section one of the bill would amend the public service law by adding a
new section 73 that would require gas and electric corporations to
provide residential customers: 1) with a credit of $25 on the balance of
their bill for each twenty-four hour period of service outage that
occurs for more than 48 consecutive hours after an emergency event; and
2) with a reimbursement up to $250 for any medication and food that
expires or spoils due to a service outage that lasts longer than 48
consecutive hours after an emergency event. Any costs incurred by the
electric or gas corporation in compliance with this section shall not be
recoverable from ratepayers.

Additionally, such corporations may petition the Public Service Commis-
sion for a waiver of the credits/reimbursement requirement's within 14
days after the occurrence of the emergency event. The corporation must
demonstrate granting of the waiver is fair, reasonable and in the public
interest. When determining whether to grant such waiver, the commission
shall consider factors such as whether the corporation complied with
their submitted emergency response plan and the hardships endured by the
customers due to the prolonged service outage

Section two of the bill would amend section 1020-f of the public author-
ities law to require the service provider contracted by the Long Island
Power Authority to offer the same reimbursements as described in Section
1 to customers. The Authority shall make any determination regarding
waivers.

Section three of this bill provides that if any provision of this act or
application to any person, corporation or circumstance is found to be
invalid, such invalidity shall not affect other provisions or applica-
tions of the act.

Section four of this bill provides the effective date.

 
DIFFERENCE BETWEEN ORIGINAL AND AMENDED VERSION (IF APPLICABLE):

N/A

 
JUSTIFICATION:

When Tropical Storm Isaias tore through New York in August of 2020, it
left behind a wake of downed trees and power lines resulting in hundreds
of thousands of customers without power. A state of emergency was
declared in Bronx, Duchess, Kings, Nassau, New York, Orange, Putnam,
Queens, Richmond, Rockland, Suffolk and Westchester counties. Yet, more
than a week later, 35,000 customers in the state were still without
power. Delayed restoration efforts caused a significant disruption to
customer's daily routines, combined with the financial loss of spoiled
food and medication.

It was later determined that inadequate storm preparations by some util-
ity companies and breakdowns in communication systems played a role in
the delayed restoration times. This bill puts rate payers first in the
event of prolonged service outage providing compensation via customer's
accounts. Simply put, if utilities fall short restoring service, custom-
ers now have recourse.

 
PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New bill.

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS FOR STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENTS:

None to the state.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect on the ninetieth day after it shall have
become law.

A.actClause:
AN ACT to amend the public service law, in relation to storm hardening and
system resiliency plans (Part A); and to amend the public service law, in
relation to providing rate payers with reimbursement following prolonged power
outages (Part B)
A.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S4824A

SPONSOR: COMRIE
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the public service law, in relation to storm hardening
and system resiliency plans (Part A); and to amend the public service
law, in relation to providing rate payers with reimbursement following
prolonged power outages (Part B)

 
PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL:

The purpose of this bill is twofold: to provide meaningful, defined
compensation to customers of gas and electric corporations experiencing
prolonged service outages and to require the submission of detailed,
forward-thinking climate change vulnerability study by utilities.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Part A amends the Public Service Law to require every combination gas
and electrical utility corporation regulated by the Public Service
Commission (PSC) to submit a climate change vulnerability study that
covers a manifest number of things to the PSC. Each plan shall explain
the approach the corporation will follow to achieve mitigate restoration
costs and reduce outage times associated with extreme weather events and
enhancing reliability. The PSC shall adopt rules to specify the elements
that must be included in a corporation's plan, and either approve or
modify said plan based on statutory criteria, such as the estimated
annual rate impact resulting from plan implementation. Each corporation
must file an updated storm plan with the PSC for approval at least every
5 years. Each corporation must file their most recently approved plan
with each county in their respective service territories. The costs for
implementing the plan may be recovered separately from such corpo-
ration's base rates as a separate annual charge, subject to approval by
the PSC in an annual proceeding if the PSC determines such costs are
fair, reasonable, and prudent.

Part B of the bill would amend the public service law by adding a new
section 73 that would require gas and electric corporations to provide
residential customers: 1) with a credit of $25 on the balance of their
bill for each twenty-four hour period of service outage that occurs for
more than 72 consecutive hours after an emergency event; and 2) with a
reimbursement for any medication and food that expires or spoils due to
a service outage that lasts longer than 72 consecutive hours after an
emergency event as well as extending all protections to small business
for food spoilage. Any costs incurred by the electric or gas corporation
in compliance with this section shall not be recoverable from ratepay-
ers.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

When Tropical Storm Isaias tore through New York in August of 2020; it
left behind a wake of downed trees and power lines resulting in hundreds
of thousands of customers without power. A state of emergency was
declared in Bronx, Duchess, Kings, Nassau, New York, Orange, Putnam,
Queens, Richmond, Rockland, Suffolk and Westchester counties. Yet, more
than a week later, 35,000 customers in the state were still without
power. Delayed restoration efforts caused a significant disruption to

customer's daily routines, combined with the financial loss of spoiled
food and medication.

It was later determined that inadequate storm preparations by some util-
ity companies and breakdowns in communication systems played a role in
the delayed restoration times. This bill puts rate payers first in the
event of prolonged service outage providing compensation via customer's
accounts. Simply put, if utilities fall short restoring service, custom-
ers now have recourse.

Similarly, due to the rise in storm intensity, dedicated storm hardening
programs need to be developed and implemented by electric utility compa-
nies throughout the State to reduce damage, restorations times, and
costs from future weather events. Storm hardening is the process of
constructing new, or upgrading old, infrastructure to increase resilien-
cy and overall reliability of service during weather events. In 2018,
Winter Storm Riley and Winter Storm Quinn greatly impacted New York's
electrical distribution system with nearly 500,000 customers losing
power.  An investigation by the Department of Public Service :recom-
mended New York's major electrical utilities create and implement storm
hardening and system resiliency plans by July 2019; however, the Public
Service Commission has been unduly slow in their approval of submitted
plan. In August 2020, Tropical Storm Isaias brought high winds, downed
trees and widespread outages to much of the state; hundreds of thousands
of customers in Long Island, New York City, Westchester and Rockland
counties experienced prolonged outages, some lasting more than a week.
Legislative hearings following these storms made it clear that storm
hardening efforts are needed to mitigate some of the impacts to the
distribution infrastructure and customers. By requiring electrical util-
ities to adopt and implement such hardening and resiliency plans and the
Public Service Commission to approve such plans within a fixed timeline,
New Yorkers will be better prepared to endure and recover from future
extreme weather events.

 
PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New bill. A Print has elements of S.4861 and S.4824.

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS FOR STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENTS:

None to the state.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
Immediate.

approvalMessage.text:
APPROVAL MEMORANDUM - No. 141 Chapter 786
 
       MEMORANDUM filed with Senate Bill Number 4824-A, entitled:
 
    "AN  ACT to amend the public service law, in relation to storm hard-
        ening and system resiliency plans (Part A);  and  to  amend  the
        public  service  law,  in relation to providing rate payers with
        reimbursement following prolonged power outages (Part B)"
 
    APPROVED
 
  Part A of this bill would amend the  Public  Service  Law  to  require
combination  gas  and  electric  corporations (electric corporations) to
prepare a Climate Change Vulnerability Study  (Study)  to  evaluate  the
electric  corporation's  electric  transmission and distribution infras-
tructure, design specifications, and procedures to understand  potential
vulnerabilities  to climate-driven risks. It will also identify adaption
measures to address vulnerabilities and other information deemed  neces-
sary by the Public Service Commission (PSC). Thereafter, electric corpo-
rations  are required to file with the PSC and serve on specified stake-
holders a "Climate Resilience Plan" (Resilience  Plan).  The  plan  must
address  storm  hardening and resilience measures for the next 10 and 20
years; explain the electric corporation's approach to mitigating impacts
from climate change  to  utility  infrastructure,  reducing  restoration
costs  and  outage  times  associated  with  extreme weather events, and
enhancing reliability; detail how the electric corporation will incorpo-
rate climate change into its planning, design, operations, and emergency
response; and incorporate climate change  into  existing  processes  and
practices,  manage  climate change risks, and build resilience. The bill
would authorize PSC to  approve  or  modify  an  electric  corporation's
proposed  Resilience  Plan  based on specified criteria within 11 months
from filing after a public hearing. Part A would also authorize an elec-
tric corporation to make an annual filing  to  recover  Resilience  Plan
costs through a charge "separate and apart from" from its base rates.
 
  Part  B  of  the  bill  would  establish a process to require electric
corporations to provide bill credits to residential and  small  business
customers,  and  compensation to such customers for certain losses after
service outages, as further described in the bill.
 
  I fully support the intent of this bill, which is to help ensure  that
the State's electric corporations take meaningful action to plan for and
adapt  to the impacts of climate change by making their electric systems
more resilient, which will in turn reduce damage to utility  infrastruc-
ture  from  weather  events  and  other climate impacts, reduce electric
system repair costs and  service  outage  times,  and  enhance  electric
service reliability across the state.
 
  Under my administration, New York is taking decisive action to respond
to threats posed by climate change and to increase resilience. For exam-
ple:
 
  Earlier  this month I announced a $1.85 million resiliency project for
Dockside Park in the Village of Cold Spring to help that community with-
stand severe storms and flooding on the Hudson River.
 
  In November, I announced the start of construction of a  $400  million
Suffolk  County  coastal  resiliency initiative that includes wastewater
 
conveyance and treatment upgrades and sewer connections  for  more  than
5,000  homes  to  mitigate  contamination  of Long Island waterways from
nitrogen and septic systems, conditions that are exacerbated by flooding
from  major  storm  events.  I also announced the launch of a multi-year
study - New York State Climate  Impacts  Assessment:  Understanding  and
Preparing  for  Our  Changing Climate - a collaborative climate research
effort led by the New York State Energy Research and Development Author-
ity to explore how climate change affects communities,  ecosystems,  and
New York's economy.
 
  In  October,  on the anniversary of Superstorm Sandy, I announced that
the Governor's Office of Storm Recovery will begin construction on a $14
million project to protect the most at-risk sections  of  Fresh  Creek's
shoreline  in  Canarsie,  Brooklyn.  The project will help the community
adapt to the effects of  climate  change  by  reducing  flooding  during
future  storms  and  rises  in sea-level, and help the area recover more
quickly from future storm events.
 
  During Climate Week, I announced the opening of the $8.3 million Envi-
ronmental Education and Resiliency Center at Hempstead Lake  State  Park
in  Nassau County, which offers hands-on learning on the topics of storm
resiliency and environmental management; provides  space  for  community
outreach; and serves as an emergency coordination center during disaster
response.
 
  The  bill's directive that each electric corporation develop a Resili-
ence Plan is another example of how New York is  leading  in  the  fight
against  climate change and I commend the bill's sponsors for addressing
this critically important component of the fight in this legislation.
 
  However, I have concerns that the part  of  the  bill  authorizing  an
electric  corporation  to make annual filings to recover Resilience Plan
costs through a charge that would be entirely separate  and  apart  from
utility  base  rates  would impose significant administrative burdens on
the Department of Public Service.  It  would  result  in  new,  unfunded
costs, and is unnecessary to achieve the purposes of this bill.
 
  I have reached an agreement with the Legislature on amendments to this
bill  that  will  authorize  electric corporations to recover Resilience
Plan costs through established cost recovery mechanisms where PSC deter-
mines costs are prudently incurred. For transparency, the PSC will iden-
tify in any order approving or modifying an electric corporation's  rate
plan  the  resiliency  and  storm  hardening  component  of  the revenue
requirement on a cost or percentage basis. So as not to delay resiliency
projects, the amendments will also  allow  an  electric  corporation  to
apply  for recovery of costs for resiliency projects placed into service
prior to base rates being reset in the first rate  proceeding  commenced
by  an  electric corporation after the PSC's approval or modification of
the corporation's Resilience Plan, through a separate charge  that  must
be detailed in a PSC filing that would also propose a method of allocat-
ing  costs.  The  amendments  will  also  make some technical changes to
improve the bill's implementation.

  Based on this agreement, I am pleased to approve this bill.
 
  The bill is approved.                          (signed) KATHY HOCHUL
 
                                ______

summary: Requires each electric corporation to submit a storm hardening and system resiliency plan to the public service commission for review and approval; makes related provisions (Part A); requires utility companies to reimburse customers for certain widespread prolonged outages; prohibits utility companies from recovering from customers the costs incurred due to power outage reimbursements; authorizes utility companies to petition the public service commission for a waiver of the reimbursement requirements (Part B).
title: Provides for storm hardening and system resiliency plans, and requires utility companies to reimburse customers for certain widespread prolonged outages
